where in M is written ἀλλ᾽ ἁλιστόνοις γύποδας | χρίμπτουσα ῥαχίαισιν [but with sea-groaning vultures' feet | grazing the rocky shores], which Turnebus corrected by restoring πόδας [feet], rightly, except that he should have written πόδα [foot], as I said under πούς [foot]. From the corrupt γύποδας [vultures' feet] the Byzantine scholiasts invented a people called Γυπόδων [the Gypodes], although a different reading γε πόδας [at least feet] is recorded. The scribe had written γύποδας [vultures' feet] with his eyes straying to γύας [fields], which ends line 708: about which I spoke in the Preface to the London edition of Prometheus (1866) p. VII.
grazing her foot on the sea-groaning rocky shores
but with sea-groaning vultures' feet | grazing the rocky shores

Thus I corrected a slight error of the Medicean manuscript μὴ χαρίζεσθαι [not to be gratified], about which see what I said in Fleckeisen's Annals 1863 vol. 87 p. 83-84. The grammarians explain the verb ῥαχίζειν [to split] by διακόπτειν [to cut through], which itself is also not rarely said of interrupted speech, about which I spoke in the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 1188, where can be added διακόπτειν τὸ συνεχὲς τοῦ λόγου [to cut through the continuity of speech], which Clement of Alexandria said p. 829. Moreover, Aeschylus, as far as I know, first and alone used a similar metaphor below, line 505: πολλῶν ῥαγεισῶν ἐλπίδων [many hopes having been shattered].
They struck with fragments of ruins, they split.
He urged that the ordinance of fire not be broken.
